Introduction - September 2010 











##### **Introduction** 

In line with our expectations, following the price rise in late July and early August, the few weeks that followed the release of our previous Base Metals One Year Forecast prices saw a modest retracement.  In part this was a reflection of the seasonal lull noted in investor activity during August. Elsewhere, a series of news which seemed unfavourable to the outlook for both mature economies and China during the month caused concern towards the outlook for indus

trial metals’ consumption. GFMS’ base metals index dropped from a peak of 300.89 on 9th August (the highest level since late April) to 277.64 on the 25th. This trend was reversed at the end of August/early September primarily due to confidence towards the outlook for Chinese consumption having been rejuvenated. On 1st September in particular, following the bullish release of the country’s manufacturing PMI estimates for August, our index rose back to close to 300. ###### The last few weeks have for yet another time confirmed the importance China continues to bear on base metals markets. The declines suffered by prices during much of August were undoubtedly at least in part triggered by the series of unfavourable news and indicators that emerged from the country (some of these are discussed in detail further on), that rocked investors’ confidence towards China’s ability to continue grow consumption at healthy rates. In contrast, as sentiment towards the world’s largest consumer of industrial metals improved more recently, prices rose dramatically, despite conditions in the United States and Europe continuing to look problematic. ###### **~~Base Metals & Other Commodity Prices~~** 250

###### **Tin and zinc the star performers in August** Looking among the six main LME metals, the prices of which performing best during August were clearly tin and zinc. The former peaked at just under $21,750/tonne on the 17th, nearly 10% on the level it started the month at and, more importantly, managed to maintain most of this gain, currently standing well above $21,000/tonne. Zinc rose a more modest 6% to its $2,129/tonne peak on 9th August, suffered more limited corrections than most other metals and has more recently recovered to levels around the August high. As discussed in the individual sections, the rally in tin prices is well supported by the fundamentals, while the improvement for zinc tends to reflect positive sentiment towards the sector rather than its individual fundamentals. ###### **Outlook to the fourth quarter looks positive, but weakness may ensue in the first half of 2011** We remain constructive towards base metals prices over the last four months of the year. Although sentiment towards mature economies remains cautious, we continue to see a material slow-down being avoided before the end of this year. Elsewhere, most indicators suggest that China continues to expand strongly. As such, we continue to predict positive year-on-year increases in base metals consumption for both the third and last quarter of the year and in most cases our forecasts also show quarter-on-quarter increases taking place. As production is also expected to increase, the overall fundament

al picture is mixed, with some markets, such as copper and tin, expected to tighten materially, while others, such as aluminium, remaining awash with excess supply. ###### **~~Base Metals Prices in Major Currencies~~** 250

LME|**491**|**84**|**54**|**9**|**345**|**7.5**|**2.5**|**6.0**|**0.6**|**2.8**|**3.0**| Independent - Informed - International **I4** Economic Indicators - September 2010 ##### **Economic Indicators** ###### **PMI’s rally to support the market** In the August Base Metals One Year Forecast, we noted that “China is at the forefront of economic concerns”. These concerns were alleviated somewhat by the release of the August PMI for China, which saw the index return over the critical 50 level (marking the difference between expansion and contraction) rising to 51.4 from 49.4 in July. The market took the figure as evidence of a managed slowdown in growth rather than a meltdown. In India, the HSBC PMI dropped slightly to 57.2 in August, pointing to continued strength in demand. The Indian economy grew 8.8% in the second quarter, the fastest rate since early 2008. It should be noted that the indicators in the more mature Asian economies are less encouraging for the base metal producers. The HSBC index for Taiwan fell below 50 for the first time in 18 months, sliding 1.3 points to 49.2 in August. Last month, growth in orders for Taiwan’s exports slowed more than expected due to falling global demand, with an easing of inventory restocking. Due to subdued demand for exports, stalled domestic consumption and the surging yen, the

ors - September 2010 The US indicators also provide support with the ISM index remaining both well above 50 and staging a rebound in August to 56.3 from 55.5 in July. This served to (temporarily) allay the growing fears of a double-dip recession. However, the latest ISM release does contain some worrying features. New orders fell from 53.5 to 53.1, while inventories rose by 1.2 points to 51.4. The gap between new export and import orders suggests trade will provide little support, if any, to growth this quarter. Consumer confidence also registered gains. The Conference Board index rebounded in August, following declines in June and July, increasing last month to 53.5 from 51. The expectations component led the gain as it had led previous declines. It rose to 72.5 from 67.5. Weaker assessments of labour market conditions contributed to the decline in assessments of current conditions to 26.9 from 29.4. The other key measure of consumer confidence in the United States, the University of Michigan index, rose by 1 point to 68.9, after weakness earlier in the summer. Compared with July, the increase was led by the current conditions component, though the expectations component also grew. Confidence also registered an uptick in the Euro zone, with the region’s sentiment index increasing to 101.8 in August from 101.1 in July. The Euro zone economic sentiment index rose from 101.1 to 101.8 in August, which is the third consecutive increase. The index is now at its highest level since March 2008. However, high unemployment and the need for fiscal tightening could undermine confidence as the year develops. The recent indicators are more upbeat than the OECD leading indicators which were released earlier in August. The latest figures (up to June) show that the OECD composite leading indicators decreased by 0.1 to 103.4. The CLIs for France and Italy point to below-trend growth in the coming months, whilst that for the U.K. points to a peak in the pace of expansion. Despite this, in many European countries, GDP has yet to return to its pre-crisis level. The sovereign debt crisis is forcing the euro zone’s peripheral countries to adopt fiscal austerity measures, increasing the risk of a double-dip recession in belt-tightening countries. Slower growth in the United States, Japan and Europe will weigh on the global economic recovery but is not expected to derail expansion in Asia and Latin America. Independent - Informed - International **E2** Copper - September 2010 ##### **Copper** ###### **Recent developments** - **_Copper prices rocketed in late August/early September and currently stand comfortably above $7,600/tonne, driven by buoyancy towards the outlook for copper consumption in China as well as, to a lesser extent, mature economies._** - **_Reported inventories fell further over the course of August, although the decline was more limited than in previous months. At end-July, LME stocks stood had fallen below 400,000 tonnes, 14,300 tonnes lower than at end-July. The decline was partly offset by a 6,000 tonne drop in Shanghai Futures Exchange (SHFE) stocks._** - **_Copper semis production in China posted a month-on-month decline in July, although the figure remained up strongly year-on-year._** ###### **Outlook for the next 12 months** - **_We continue to see prices trend upwards over the rest of the year. A visible improvement in copper’s fundamentals, as consumption growth receives a boost by restocking in mature economies and China continues to boom, is expected to perpetuate investor interest in the red metal._** - **_Conditions are expected to worsen materially in the first half of next year. Plagued by fiscal imbalances, growth in mature economies is expected to slow and this may also be augmented by a tighter Chinese monetary policy. By the second quarter, we expect a (brief) return to surplus._** - **_Coupled by a general tendency to liquidate risky assets, the above change in fundamental conditions is expected to halt copper’s rally. At the same time, the metal’s bullish longerterm outlook will probably see strong support developing

at corrections below $7,000/tonne._** - **_Our alternative scenarios’ projections remain broadly unchanged from the previous edition of our Forecasting Monthly. Under Scenario B, undisturbed growth in demand sees prices establish themselves above $8,000/tonne (on a sustainable basis) before the end of this year. In contrast, the double-dip conditions of Scenario B sees prices trend downwards over the next twelve months._** ###### **~~GFMS’ Forecast Scenarios~~** ###### **Base Case, 50% Probability** Represents what GFMS consider the most likely outcome for the markets. ###### **Scenario B, 20% Probability** - **_Risks to the downside remain significant, given the high involvement of speculators in the market, but we would expect any corrections to prove short-lived._** |**~~Copper Supply-D~~**|**~~emand~~**

Independent - Informed - International **C1** Copper - September 2010 ###### **Market background** The weeks that followed the release of our last Base Metals One Year Forecast saw copper prices move sideways and towards the end of the month in particular losing much of the gains they had achieved in late July and early August. Once again, the market’s immediate fundamentals had a secondary role in this move and it was investor selling on the back of future expectations that largely drove the decline. This is turn was driven by concerns about the outlook for copper consumption as a series of unfavourable economic indicators emerged. Added to this were seasonal factors, such as the exit from risky positions in advance of any summer vacations and the decline of activity overall, resulting in thin volumes and exaggerated price moves. As a result, on 25th August, copper prices bottomed at $7,067/ tonne, compared to peaks above $7,400/tonne earlier in the month. The tide changed at the turn of the month, as a series of positive news on the Chinese and, to a lesser extent, the US economy, notabl

y the rebound in both countries’ manufacturing PMIs on 1st September boosted investor sentiment, helping the cash price breaking through the $7,600/tonne mark for the first time since April (on an official LME quote basis). The copper price correction and recovery were both in line with GFMS’ expectations and our view on copper for the next twelve months remain virtually unchanged from our previous monthly. Specifically, we continue to see a general uptrend over the remainder of 2010, as copper’s fundamentals improve, while we acknowledge that corrections will remain a feature of the market, given the ongoing high involvement of speculators. Moreover, we continue to expect weaker supply-demand conditions in the first half of 2011 keeping prices under control, with more noteworthy gains not taking place until the second half of next year. ###### **LME stocks fall through 400,000 tonnes but draw-down slows** LME inventories continued to fall during August, although the declines were more limited than during the previous months, probably at least in part due to the slow-down in the Chinese stockpiling we have noted in the last few months having continued. By end-month stocks amounted to a little less than 399,000 tonnes, down by 14,300 tonne on the end-July figure and at their lowest since November 2009. Stocks held at SHFE listed warehouses posted their first monthly increase since April, amounting to a modest 6,000 tonnes, ending the month at a little less than 111,000 tonnes. ###### **Chinese demand suffers a seasonal month-on-month decline, but remains up year-on-year** The latest official data suggest Chinese copper semis production fell by 8% on a month-on-month basis, in line with the seasonal norm. On a year-on-year basis, the picture continued to look bullish, with semis production rising by around a fifth, to around 867,000 tonnes. Against this, reported consumption of refined copper, defined as the sum of production, net imports of metal and net draw on reported stocks, fell by a more contained 3% month-on-month and was only marginally up compared to last year, at around 631,000 tonnes. (We note here that the year-on-year comparison suffers from distortions in the 2009 base, caused by the dramatic stockpiling of metal that was taking place in the country during that time.) The month-on-month decline in reported consumption was in part driven by the 4% fall in production, itself linked to lower imports of concentrates as well as falling mine production during the month. Elsewhere, reported inventory declines in July were more limited than in June. Partly offsetting the above, net imports of refined metal actually increased. Copper Premiums Jan 05 - Present

**C2** Independent - Informed - International Copper - September 2010 The difference between semis production and reported consumption fell on a month-on-month basis by 19%, to 237,000 tonnes. Against this, net scrap imports (using official data as derived figures are not available for July) seem to have increased, suggesting a “looser” market in July than in June. We note nevertheless that the ratio between the two remained historically low at 1:1.6. Elsewhere, a few days prior to the suspension of the Frontier operation, the International Chamber of Commerce tribunal that was examining the arbitration relating to First Quantum’s Kolwezi project (over which a dispute between the company and the government of the DRC began in late 2009), ordered the DRC government to refrain from taking action on that particular project before it reaches a decision. ###### **Mine production rises in Chile and Peru** According to the latest official statistics, copper mine production in Chile rose by 6.3% year-on-year in July to reach 454,178 tonnes. This brought total production over the first seven months of the year to 3.075 million tonnes, up little less than 2% year-on-year. Production was also higher in Peru in July, by nearly 6% year-on-year, to a little over 106,000 tonnes. In early August, a small copper-gold mine in San Jose in northern Chile collapsed, leaving 33 miners trapped inside it to this day and most likely for a few months to come. The accident has brought safety practices in the country in the spotlight and a committee has been created to review current regulations over the next three months. ###### **Soldiers seize First Quantum’s Frontier mine** Albeit dramatic, GFMS do not find these latest developments surprising and, if anything, we perceive them to be supportive of our decision to err on the side of caution in our previous forecast of Congolese copper mine production for this year. Although we had not specifically included the suspension of the Frontier mine in our projections, we had made allowances for potential disruptions in our projections. As such, we have opted not to change our full year 2010 forecast for the time being. Elsewhere in Africa, Brazilian Vale and South African African Rainbow Minerals recently started construction at Konkola North, which is expected to deliver 45,000 tonnes of copper in concentrate in its initial phase, ramping up to 100,000 tonnes in its second phase. The project is expected to start producing in 2015 and has a life-of-mine expectancy of 28 years. In late August soldiers ordered First Quantum to evacuate its Frontier mine in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), following the supreme court’s 21st May decision to transfer the mining licence and ri

ghts for the operation to government-owned Sodiminco. The company has confirmed it has suspended operations at the mine but continues to fight the decision through international arbitration. LME Stocks vs Spot Price

Independent - Informed - International **C3** Copper - September 2010 ###### **Market outlook** The recently price recovery to current levels just above $7,600/tonne was more or less within GFMS’ expectations. As such, although we would not rule out a correction in the near-term, we would expect this to be relatively short lived and prices to soon return to current levels. Moreover, we remain of the view that in the next few months there remains ample upside for copper prices, as fundamentals improve and investors become aware of the deficit that we continue to expect will be in place in the market and bid prices up. We re-iterate here that this general uptrend will almost certainly continue to be disturbed by recurring shortlived corrections, as speculators engage in active trading of the red metal. Production growth is expected to remain positive, but fall short of past targets, due to constraints such as (but not limited to) the trouble in the DRC mentioned earlier.  As a result, the quarterly deficit in the market is expected to rise to just over 100,000 tonnes over the last three months of the year. 

This buoyancy is somewhat lost in the first half of the year, as the global economic slow-down we expect will come as a result of mature economies’ fiscal woes coupled by the Chinese and Indian authorities trying to keep their economies from overheating, impacts on copper consumption.  Although we continue to see supply falling short of demand over the first quarter overall, the deficit is forecast to drop to less than a quarter of the one seen in the final quarter of this year.  Moreover, as conditions remain unfavourable to copper demand in the second quarter, we expect a short-lived return to surplus over the period. 

Moving to prices, the worsening environment will 

undoubtedly affect investor behaviour, in part through its impact on sentiment towards copper but primarily due to the general tendency to liquidate risky assets we forecast will be in place throughout much of the first six months of next year.  At the same time, given copper’s solid longer-term fundamentals, we would expect very strong bargain-hunting buying to emerge during ventures below $7,000/tonne, culminating in a solid floor in the upper $6,000s.  Moreover, we believe there will remain sufficient underlying support for short-term breaches of the $8,000/tonne mark to be repeated, on bouts of positive fundamental news.  Overall, we would expect average prices for the first and second quarter to be virtually unchanged from the $7,400/tonne average we forecast for the last quarter of this year, but that the declines will be modest.

Vale announced in early August that the Goro project, located in New Caledonia, has successfully produced its first nickel metal product. The Goro plant is now almost complete. Goro is a nickel laterite project with an estimated annual nominal capacity to produce 58,000 tonnes of nickel and 4,000 tonnes of cobalt as a by-product. Looking further ahead, Sherritt International has stated that the 5,600 tpy Ambatovey project should come on-stream in the first half of 2011. The project is 40% owned by Sherritt with Sumitomo Corp and Korea Resources Group each having 27.5% and with SNC-Lavalin holding the remaining 5%. However, the existing high pressure acid leach (HPAL) projects continue to flag the problems with this production route. Output at Murrin Murrin in the first half of this year fell by 7% year-on-year to 1,008 tonnes due to a pipeline failure at one of its autoclave circuits in May.
